simple: a written answer to "what could go wrong with this thing on purpose, and what will we do about it?"
analogy: thinking like a burglar about your own house.
precise: a structured description of a system, the threats against it and the decision taken about each threat, made by the people who build the system and kept up to date with it; organised around four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, did we do a good job.
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); the wording of the four questions is in an unverified box

simple: something worth protecting or worth attacking.
analogy: the valuables in the middle of the burglar's sheet.
precise: anything of value in or reachable through a system: data, a capability (making a robot move), or availability; some assets are stepping stones to others.
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a place where something from outside can get in.
analogy: a door, a window, a cat flap or a key under a pot.
precise: an interface through which data, commands or physical access enter a system: a network port, a radio, a button, a file the system reads, an update channel, a debug or service connector. Not the entry point of a program (F2-44).
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: all the entry points of a system together.
analogy: every door, window and hiding place of the house, counted.
precise: the set of entry points and the code and data reachable through them; reducing it removes threats instead of mitigating them one by one.
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: something bad that could happen to a system on purpose.
analogy: "a burglar comes in through the balcony".
precise: a possible harmful action against an asset by someone or something through an entry point; threat modelling works mostly at this level, before every vulnerability is known.
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a weakness that lets a threat happen.
analogy: "the balcony window does not lock".
precise: a specific flaw in design or implementation that makes a threat achievable.
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a drawing that breaks one bad goal into the smaller steps an attacker would need.
analogy: "get in" splits into "door" OR "window"; "door" needs "key" AND "nobody home".
precise: a tree whose root is an attacker goal and whose children are alternative (OR) or jointly required (AND) sub-goals; leaves carry attributes such as effort; evaluated bottom-up (OR = cheapest child, AND = sum), giving the cheapest path.
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); evaluation rules demonstrated by R1 of F11-13 (attack_tree.cpp, run in this build)

simple: something you change so that a threat becomes harder or impossible.
analogy: moving the spare key to a trusted neighbour.
precise: a design or implementation change that addresses a threat; the other decisions about a threat are to remove the feature, transfer the threat, or accept it with a written reason.
source: D1 of F11-13 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); the four decisions are in an unverified box

simple: a drawing of what moves through a system, from where to where.
analogy: a sheet showing letters, shopping and keys moving in and out of a flat as arrows.
precise: a diagram of external entities, processes, data stores and data flows, with trust boundaries drawn as dashed lines; used to answer "what are we working on?" because threats attach to its elements.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a person or system outside your control that sends or receives data.
analogy: the postman.
precise: a DFD element representing something the system interacts with but does not implement or control.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a piece of your system that does something with data.
analogy: the porter who sorts parcels.
precise: a DFD element that transforms or forwards data (a program, a service, a firmware task); not the same as an operating-system process, although one often maps onto the other.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a place where data waits.
analogy: the cupboard where parcels are kept.
precise: a DFD element that holds data at rest: a file, a database, a parameter area in flash, a log.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a line where "who is in charge" or "who can be trusted" changes.
analogy: the castle wall and its gate; the front door of a flat.
precise: a line on a DFD between elements that run with different privileges, belong to different owners or are reachable by different attackers; flows that cross it are where most threats concentrate; it exists only if a mechanism enforces it.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: six kinds of thing that can go wrong on purpose, one per letter.
analogy: six questions asked at every gate.
precise: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege; each violates one property: authentication, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability, authorization. Not the stride of memory access (HW203).
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a rule for which of the six STRIDE questions to ask about which kind of element.
analogy: you do not ask whether a cupboard can lie about its identity.
precise: a table mapping DFD element types to the STRIDE categories that usually apply (as applied in this course: external entity S, R; process all six; data store T, I, D and R for logs; data flow T, I, D), used to enumerate threats systematically.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); the table is in an unverified box (course's reading of the book's chart)

simple: pretending to be someone or something else.
analogy: a stranger claiming to be the neighbour with the spare key.
precise: a STRIDE category: a threat against authentication.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: changing data or code you should not change.
analogy: a parcel swapped on the way.
precise: a STRIDE category: a threat against integrity, of data in transit, at rest, or of code.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: denying you did something, when nobody can show otherwise.
analogy: "I never took the key".
precise: a STRIDE category: a threat against non-repudiation; answered by logs the actor cannot change and by signed requests.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: someone reading what they should not.
analogy: reading other people's letters.
precise: a STRIDE category: a threat against confidentiality.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: stopping something from working for the people who should use it.
analogy: blocking the stairs.
precise: a STRIDE category: a threat against availability; on radio links includes jamming, which no protocol prevents.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: getting more power than you were given.
analogy: the cleaner opening the locked study.
precise: a STRIDE category: a threat against authorization, for example a parser bug that lets input run code with the program's rights.
source: D1 of F11-14 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a short check value that only someone with the secret key can compute for a message.
analogy: a wax seal that only the castle's own ring can make.
precise: a value computed from a secret key and a message such that, without the key, producing a valid value for a new or changed message is infeasible; the receiver recomputes and compares; gives integrity and origin from a key holder, not secrecy, and not freshness. Not the MAC (media access controller) of networking.
source: D3 of F11-15 (NIST FIPS 180-4; IETF RFC 2104 / NIST FIPS 198-1) — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a standard way to build a MAC from a hash function.
analogy: the seal made by pressing the ring twice, in a fixed way.
precise: HMAC(K, m) = H((K xor opad) || H((K xor ipad) || m)), key padded to the hash's block size (hashed first if longer), ipad = 0x36 and opad = 0x5C repeated; for SHA-256 the block is 64 bytes and the output 32 bytes.
source: D3 of F11-15 — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); the course's implementation agrees with Python's hmac module on four inputs (R2 of F11-15, run in this build)

simple: sending again a real message that someone recorded earlier.
analogy: yesterday's sealed order handed to the guard again today.
precise: an attack in which a valid, authenticated message is captured and re-sent later or elsewhere; a MAC alone does not detect it.
source: D1 of F11-15 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); demonstrated by R3 and R4 of F11-15

simple: a test that a message is new, not a copy of an old one.
analogy: the guard keeps the number of the last order and refuses any order with a smaller number.
precise: a receiver-side rule using a monotonic counter, a timestamp or a challenge inside the authenticated message, so old or repeated messages are refused; the receiver's state must survive restarts.
source: D1 of F11-15 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); restart failure demonstrated by R4 of F11-15

simple: several independent protections, so that one failing is not the end.
analogy: the castle has a wall, a gate, guards and a keep.
precise: layers of controls with different failure modes (for a robot: authenticated commands, a speed limit in firmware, a command timeout, a hard-wired emergency stop), so that a single flaw does not lead directly to harm.
source: D1 of F11-15 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the two-way radio conversation between a drone and its ground station.
analogy: messengers riding between the castle and a scout in the field.
precise: a data link carrying status from the vehicle and commands, missions and parameters to it, usually with a message protocol such as MAVLink; distinct from the RC link.
source: D2 of F11-16 (MAVLink Developer Guide) — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the name a message gives for who sent it.
analogy: the name written on the outside of a letter.
precise: fields in each frame of a protocol like MAVLink that identify the sending system and component; claims made by the sender, not proof, unless the frame is authenticated.
source: D2 of F11-16 (MAVLink Developer Guide) — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); MAVLink field details are in an unverified box

simple: adding to every radio frame a seal that only holders of a shared key can make.
analogy: the castle's wax seal on every message the scout receives.
precise: per-frame authentication with a shared secret: a truncated keyed hash over the frame and a timestamp or counter, checked by the receiver, which also rejects frames older than the last accepted one on that stream; MAVLink 2 defines its own signing (details unverified in this build).
source: D2 of F11-16 (MAVLink Developer Guide) — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); the course's toy version is ULink (R2 of F11-16, run in this build)

simple: drowning out a radio link with noise so that nothing gets through.
analogy: someone shouting so loudly at the gate that no messenger can be heard.
precise: denial of service on a radio channel by transmitting interference; no message protocol prevents it, so the vehicle needs a link-loss failsafe; deliberate jamming is illegal in many countries.
source: D1 of F11-16 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); failsafe behaviour from F10-12's lab runs

simple: faking the satellite signals a vehicle uses to know where it is.
analogy: moving the road signs so the scout walks the wrong way.
precise: transmitting counterfeit satellite-navigation signals so that a receiver computes a wrong position or time; answered by cross-checks in the estimator and conservative failsafes.
source: D1 of F11-16 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: many users or groups sharing the same machines.
analogy: forty flats sharing one laundry room.
precise: a design where several tenants share infrastructure and are kept apart only by isolation mechanisms of different strength: file permissions, users and processes, containers, virtual machines, separate nodes.
source: D1 of F11-17 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: someone who is allowed in and can still do harm.
analogy: a neighbour in the laundry room.
precise: an attacker who holds legitimate access to part of a system, or controls something that does (a stolen account, a malicious dependency); in a cluster, the default assumption for every other user.
source: D1 of F11-17 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: using one machine you got into to reach the next.
analogy: from the laundry room through an unlocked door to the caretaker's office.
precise: the steps an attacker takes after a first foothold, along network paths and trust relationships, towards more valuable assets; a reachability analysis lists the paths that exist.
source: D1 of F11-17 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open); reachability demonstrated by R2 of F11-17

simple: the separate network that controls the machines themselves.
analogy: the caretaker's office with the master key and the fuse boxes.
precise: the network that reaches the BMCs (and switch and storage management interfaces) of a cluster: power control, remote console and firmware update for every node.
source: C3 of F11-17 (OS305, DS304 chapters of this university) — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: give each person and program only the access it needs.
analogy: the cleaner gets the key to the laundry room, not the master key.
precise: a design principle: every component runs with the smallest set of rights that lets it do its job, so its compromise exposes as little as possible; limits elevation of privilege.
source: D1 of F11-17 (Adam Shostack, "Threat Modeling: Designing for Security") — pending verification (sources title only, dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a setting that removes permissions from every new file you make.
analogy: a rule that every bag left in the laundry room is closed unless you open it on purpose.
precise: a per-process mask of permission bits; a file or directory created with requested mode m gets m & ~umask (0666 & ~0022 = 0644; 0666 & ~0077 = 0600).
source: D4 of F11-17 (IEEE Std 1003.1 / The Open Group Base Specifications, POSIX) — pending verification (title only, dossier gate G1 open); behaviour shown by R3 of F11-17 (umask_demo.sh, run in this build)
